title: India's Infrastructure Budget Has Nearly Doubled in Five Years. It Is Now the Largest Public Works Push in the Country's History.
excerpt: Rs 12.2 trillion earmarked for FY26 covers highways, railways, semiconductors, and a bullet train that is 80 percent finished. The strategy: spend first, attract private capital after.
body:
The numbers tell a story that India's roads and rail lines are only beginning to show. Government spending on highways, railways, and semiconductor manufacturing has nearly doubled over the past five years, with a record Rs 12.2 trillion ($147 billion) earmarked for FY26, according to a Nikkei Asia report released this week.

Public works expenditure hit Rs 11 trillion in the fiscal year that ended in March. The new allocation represents the largest infrastructure outlay in India's history — and the strategy behind it is deliberate: spend public money first, and use the roads, rails, and fabs to pull in private capital after.

## The Bullet Train Is 80 Percent Done

The flagship project that once drew skeptics is now a construction fact. The Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail corridor — India's first bullet train — has crossed the 80 percent completion mark, with more than 400 of its approximately 500 kilometres of elevated track in place.

Japan is funding around 80 percent of the project cost through concessional yen loans, making it one of the largest bilateral infrastructure financing deals in Asia. When operational, the train will cut the Mumbai-Ahmedabad journey to roughly two hours from the current five to seven by road.

## Highways and the Ganga Expressway

Road development remains the backbone of the infrastructure push. The government is accelerating national highway construction to keep pace with a rapidly urbanizing economy, and the showpiece project is the Ganga Expressway in Uttar Pradesh — a 594-kilometre corridor running along the Ganges basin with a price tag of Rs 360 billion.

Prime Minister Modi, inaugurating a section in April, described it as "a new lifeline for the state's development." The expressway will connect Meerut to Prayagraj, cutting through a region with more than 200 million people and some of the weakest road connectivity in northern India.

## Semiconductors: The Next Frontier

The infrastructure push now extends beyond physical transport. India's semiconductor ambitions — catalyzed by the $10 billion incentive scheme announced in 2023 — are materializing in the form of fabrication units in Gujarat and Assam. The Tata-PSMC fab near Ahmedabad and the Micron packaging facility in Sanand are among the first facilities to break ground.

The bet is strategic: India wants to reduce its near-total dependence on imported chips, which currently cost the economy over $10 billion annually in imports. The semiconductor allocation is folded into the broader public works figure, signaling that the government sees chip manufacturing as infrastructure, not industry policy.

## The Growth Flywheel

India's economy recorded 7.7 percent growth in FY25, driven by both infrastructure spending and resilient consumer demand. The World Bank this week upgraded India's GDP forecast while downgrading nearly everyone else, projecting 6.6 percent growth for the current year.

The infrastructure push is designed to sustain this momentum. Better roads reduce logistics costs — currently around 14 percent of GDP, compared to 8 percent in the United States. Faster rail reduces the pressure on highways and airports. Semiconductor fabs reduce import dependency. Each investment is meant to unlock the next.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, the infrastructure transformation is not abstract. NRIs visiting home are already noticing the difference — new expressways where potholed state highways once crawled, metro systems in second-tier cities, and airports that did not exist five years ago.

The investment implications are equally concrete. Infrastructure bonds, real estate along new corridors, and the growing ecosystem of construction and engineering firms are creating a new layer of investable India that did not exist at this scale a decade ago.

The concrete is being poured. The question is no longer whether India will build. It is whether the country can build fast enough to match the ambition its budget has laid down.
